input:
Partial miscibility is a term that is used to describe the behaviour of certain pairs of liquids that dissolve in one another only to a limited extent. When two such liquids are brought together in proportions that lie within the range of limited miscibility, they do not merge into a single uniform liquid phase. Instead, the mixture separates into two distinct liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and holding the second only up to its solubility limit, the other rich in the second liquid on the same basis, and the two phases coexist in a state of equilibrium with one another.

The condition that governs this equilibrium can be expressed in words, without the need for any equation. For each component that is present in the system, the chemical potential of that component must have the same value in both of the phases. The chemical potential may be thought of as a driving force for the transfer of a component between the phases: if the chemical potential of a component is higher in one phase than it is in the other, that component tends to move from the first phase into the second, and the movement will go on until the difference between the two potentials has been eliminated. At equality there is no net tendency for transfer in either direction, and the system is at equilibrium. It should be noted that this condition must be satisfied for each component individually, and equality in the case of one component does not by itself guarantee equality in the case of the other.

A further consequence is that the compositions of the two phases are determined by the equilibrium itself. At any given temperature and pressure, each phase has a definite composition that does not depend on the proportions in which the liquids were mixed in the first place. If the proportions of the overall mixture are altered, the compositions of the individual phases remain the same, as long as the mixture remains within the two-phase range, and what changes instead is the relative amount of each phase that is present. Beyond the limits of that range, the liquids dissolve in one another completely, only a single phase is formed, and the considerations described here no longer apply.
target:
Partial miscibility is the behaviour of a pair of liquids that dissolve in one another only to a limited extent. Mixed in the proportions that fall inside the miscibility gap, such a pair does not form a single homogeneous liquid. It separates into two liquid phases, one phase rich in the first liquid and holding the second only up to its limit of solubility, the other phase rich in the second liquid on the same terms, and the two phases rest in contact in equilibrium with each other.

The condition for that equilibrium is stated here in words, as the passage uses no equation for it. For every component of the pair, the chemical potential of the component is equal in the two phases. Chemical potential is the quantity whose difference drives transfer: a component moves from the phase in which its chemical potential stands higher to the phase in which it stands lower, and the movement continues until the difference is gone. At equality there is no driving force in either direction, and no net transfer of the component takes place. The condition holds component by component: equality for one component does not settle the other, and both equalities stand together in the equilibrium state.

The equilibrium fixes what each phase contains. At a given temperature and pressure the composition of each phase is set by the condition itself, and not by the proportions in which the two liquids were poured together. A mixture made up with more of the first liquid than another holds the same two phase compositions as that other mixture, as long as both mixtures fall inside the gap; what changes is the amount of each phase present, the phase rich in the added liquid growing at the expense of the other. Outside the gap the pair dissolves completely, a single phase forms, and the question of equilibrium between phases does not arise. Inside the gap, the two-phase state with equal chemical potentials is the state the mixture reaches and the state it keeps.
